extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of philosophy and history of science (readers studying Bacon and the reaction against Aristotelian method)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the methodological principles and evaluative standards associated with Francis Bacon (and his precursors), especially those contrasted with Aristotelian practice. The page lists and discusses specific desiderata for scientific method and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consulting and collecting facts; going straight to Nature; instituting observations and experiments before formulating general propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the emphasis with which he insisted on the necessity of consulting and collecting facts, of going straight to Nature, of instituting observations and experiments before formulating general propositions’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a central feature of Bacon's method — prioritize direct observation and experiment as the foundation for forming general claims, rather than beginning from abstract principles or received doctrine. The surrounding text contrasts this with scholastic reliance on authority and idle subtleties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual ascent from propositions or axioms of lower to higher generality
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the gradual ascent from propositions or axioms of a lower to those of a higher degree of generality’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological rule: build general theories stepwise from less general, well-established propositions rather than leaping to sweeping axioms. The page frames this as part of Bacon's distinct approach to induction and theory-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and comparison of instances in place of Inductio per Enumerationem Simplem
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the selection and comparison of instances in place of the old Inductio per Enumerationem Simplicem’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than relying on simple exhaustive enumeration of cases, the method recommends selecting and comparing illustrative instances (including contrasting and negative instances) to discriminate causes and form reliable generalisations. The text notes Aristotle's notion of Inductio Completa is impracticable and that selection/salient comparison is necessary in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disregard of Authority
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scientific attitude that does not treat ancient or established authors (e.g., Aristotle) as final arbiters of truth. The page repeatedly emphasises that doctrines should be judged by evidence/experience rather than by deference to authoritative names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint of Fancy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against speculative imagination uncontrolled by observation and experiment. Fancy should be restrained so that hypotheses are disciplined by empirical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction must be from particulars; ultimate major premiss rests on induction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Aristotle bases all evidence ultimately on the observation of individual facts... the ultimate major premiss of any train of deductive reasoning must itself rest on an induction from particulars.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: general claims require grounding in observed particulars. The text also warns that the ideal of exhaustive induction (Inductio Completa) is normally unattainable, so practical induction requires careful selection of instances and attention to negative cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have regard to causal connexion when framing generalisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle and later writers ‘shew… the importance of having regard to causal connexion in framing our generalisations’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming generalisations, prioritise instances that illuminate causal relations; compare positive and negative instances to isolate causal factors. The page cites Aristotle (De Partibus Animalium iv.2) as recognizing negative instances and causal connection — a point Bacon amplifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of sensory experience and experiment in producing knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Fit ergo ex sensu memoria; ex memoria multorum saepius iterata, experimentum; ab experimentis scientiae aut artis ratio manat.’ (John of Salisbury quoted) — sensory perception → memory → experiment → science
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stipulation that sensory experience is the condition (if not source) of knowledge: sense impressions lead to memory, repeated memories produce experiment, and experiments give rise to scientific understanding. The text uses medieval and Roger Bacon passages to justify experimental primacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as ascent from effects to causes and descent from causes to effects
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Physical science ascends from effects to causes, and descends again from causes to effects.’ (attributed to Richard of St. Victor)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended investigatory pattern: derive causal hypotheses from observed effects, then test and apply those causal understandings back to predict or explain effects. The page notes Bacon perceived the practical value of this two-way movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read authorities with diligence and judgment; do not accept dicta without other proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice reflected in opponents’ cautions: ‘the works of Aristotle should be frequently read, sed cum diligenti consideratione atque judicio’ and Cabaeus: if we rely solely on Aristotle’s dicta without independent proof, we do not follow his doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical admonition: consult classical/authoritative texts but always subject them to critical scrutiny and independent empirical verification rather than uncritical acceptance.
